How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX (Principal Appellant), XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX (co-Appellant) and their daughters, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX and XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXXAssociate Appellants) are appealing a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) dated July 16, 2018, rejecting their claims for refugee protection.

The Appellants' primary allegation is that the co-Appellant, a citizen of Jordan, was threatened by a man from a powerful family after she attempted to make a police complaint for harassment against him. The Appellants' primary residence was in Saudi Arabia. All of the Appellants, except the co-Appellant, are stateless Palestinians. The co-Appellant holds Jordanian citizenship though she has rarely resided there. The co-Appellant and her daughters travelled to Jordan in XXXX 2016. The Principal Appellant remained in Saudi Arabia. While on that trip, her daughter XXXX was sexually harassed by a man in a shopping mall. They reported the incident to the police where they were allegedly dissuaded from pressing charges because the assailant is from a powerful family. When the co-Appellant insisted, the family allegedly suffered reprisals. When the Principal Appellant tried to join them in Jordan, he was questioned by the Jordanian authorities about the validity of his travel document. The Appellants claim that the assailant influenced the Jordanian authorities to question him as retaliation for the sexual harassment charges. The co-Appellant allegedly received a phone call stating that the questions about the Principal Appellant's passport were the first move and warning her to take care of her daughters while they are crossing the road, lest they be involved in an accident. Fearing for their lives at the hands of the sexual harasser, the Appellants left Jordan and arrived in Canada on September 1, 2016 where they requested protection.

The RPD found that the stateless Appellants' country of former habitual reference is Saudi Arabia and evaluated their claims accordingly. It found that they had not established a fear of persecution against that country. It also found that the co-Appellant had not demonstrated that the sexual harasser's family had or could unduly influence the Jordanian state protection apparatus and that she was not at risk of harm in Jordan for her gender. The Appellants argue that the RPD failed to grasp the nature of the persecution that the stateless Appellants face in Saudi Arabia and that it misapprehended key evidence relating to the co-Appellant's fear in Jordan.

The appeal is denied. The determinative issue for the stateless Appellants is whether they have established a well-founded fear of persecution in Saudi Arabia. The determinative issue for the co-Appellant is whether she has established the credibility of her claim in Jordan. The Principal Appellant left Saudi Arabia to join his wife in Jordan, not because he is being persecuted by the Saudi state. The stateless Appellants have not demonstrated that they suffered persecution by virtue of their nationality as Palestinians or their stateless status. The co-Appellant has not established that the sexual harasser's family can influence the Jordanian state apparatus in order to persecute her and has not established that she is at risk in Jordan due to her gender.

The Appellants are requesting a hearing pursuant to Section 110(6) of the IRPA. I can only hold a hearing if new evidence is raised under Section 110(4) of IRPA. Since no new evidence has been filed, the request for a hearing is denied. ANALYSIS Credibility Claims against Saudi Arabia

Other than the co-Appellant, whose country of citizenship is Jordan, the Appellants are stateless Palestinians with Jordanian travel documents. These travel documents do not confer citizenship upon the Appellants. Both the Appellants and I agree that the RPD correctly identified Saudi Arabia as the country of former habitual reference for the Palestinian appellants.

The RPD correctly concluded that the Principal Appellant's loss of his residency status is related to the termination of his work contract in Saudi Arabia and that the termination of that contract does not amount to persecution.1

The Appellants argue that the RPD erred by making negative credibility findings without providing sufficient reasons for those findings, that it misconstrued the nature of the persecution that the stateless Appellants suffer in Saudi Arabia and that it erred in concluding that the Principal Appellant would not be denied re-entry to Saudi Arabia on a balance of probabilities.

The Principal Appellant claims that he lost his job due to the "Saudization" policies which prioritize offering employment to citizens of Saudi Arabia over foreign workers. As a stateless Palestinian, he alleges that he cannot return to Saudi Arabia because his work contract was not renewed. The RPD found that he did not reliably and satisfactorily explain the timing of the loss of his job in Saudi Arabia and drew a negative inference about his credibility. He alleges that the RPD erred by failing to justify and explain the negative credibility finding and that it is in essence an implausibility finding. He submits that the loss of his job in light of the "Saudization" policies is a reality that falls within the realm of possibilities.

I agree that the Principal Appellant's job loss as a result of "Saudization" policies is plausible and credible. I also agree that the RPD erred because it did not explain why it found his explanations to be credible. The RPD simply listed its objection, mentioned the Principal Appellant's explanations and concluded that he was not credible.2 The RPD should have explained why the explanations were not acceptable.

After considering the Principal Appellant's testimony and the evidence on the record, I find that he has not established that he lost his job due to the "Saudization" of the economy in Saudi Arabia. His employment termination letter states that the company closed the Eastern Region branch office where he worked.3 Though he testified that he believes that his termination was related to the "Saudization" policies, I find that he is merely speculating that "Saudization" is the cause. In other testimony, he confirmed that the branch office in question was, in fact, downsized. The evidence causes me to conclude that on a balance of probabilities, the Principal Appellant lost his job due to downsizing and not due to any discrimination related to his foreign status and his nationality.

Despite my finding, I also find that even if the Principal Appellant lost his job due to the "Saudization" of the economy, it is not akin to persecution. As a sovereign nation, the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia has the right to establish employment policies to the benefit of its citizens. It is not persecutory for an employer not to renew an employment contract to respect those policies. Nothing in the record establishes that the Principal Appellant could not have secured other employment in Saudi Arabia.

Though the RPD commented that it was not persuaded that the Principal Appellant would be denied re-entry to Saudi Arabia, that is not the issue at hand. To ensure that a claimant properly qualifies for Convention refugee status, the Board is compelled to ask itself why the applicant is being denied entry to a country of former habitual residence because the reason for the denial may, in certain circumstances, constitute an act of persecution by the state. The issue, therefore, is whether the Board asked itself this question.4

Ultimately, at issue is the reason why the Principal Appellant left Saudi Arabia. The loss of a job is not in and of itself persecutory and does not fall into the realm of justifications for that reason only. The Principal Appellant testified that he left Saudi Arabia to join his wife in Jordan, not because he could not find a job nor because the Saudi authorities specifically asked him to leave. I consider that his departure was voluntary. If the Principal Appellant is denied re-entry to Saudi Arabia, it will be because he does not have a valid residency permit following the loss of his job. His departure was not related to his Palestinian nationality for reasons of persecution related to convention Grounds, a risk to his life, a risk of cruel or unusual treatment or punishment or a risk of torture.

The Principal Appellant argues that the RPD failed to grasp why his job loss and inability to return to Saudi Arabia is persecutory as a stateless Palestinian, which he contends is different from the situation of other foreigners who have countries of nationality to return to. I note that this argument was not presented before the RPD, but I will address it in this decision nonetheless.

The Appellants argue that their statelessness is the source of the harm that they are suffering in Saudi Arabia. In fact, documentary evidence provided by the Appellants establishes that the history and citizenship policy surrounding stateless Palestinians is complex and is related to colonial intervention in the region as well as efforts by Palestinian leaders to exert control over the policy and practices of historically Palestinian territories.5 Other documentary evidence provided by the Appellants establishes that there are people of Palestinian descent who are citizens of Jordan.6 However, Ex-Gazan Palestinians are not considered citizens for historical policy reasons. The stateless Appellants fall into this category and are treated as Arab foreign nationals by Jordanian authorities. The Kingdom of Saudi Arabia has not rendered the Appellants stateless and is not refusing their entry into the country because they are stateless Palestinians. If the Principal Appellant and his family are refused entry, it will be because the Principal Appellant has not secured a work contract allowing the country to issue him a residency permit, on a balance of probabilities.7 The stateless situation has not been caused by Saudi Arabia in that the Principal Appellant was born in that country as a Palestinian national and cannot seek citizenship there due to laws which apply to all foreigners, stateless or not. While the Appellants are not in a satisfying situation, and while being stateless does expose them to discriminatory treatment in Saudi Arabia, the situation is not persecutory. The Appellants are subject to the same restrictions that are placed upon non-citizens. Being stateless means that they cannot benefit from a state of Palestine where they might enjoy some of the positive discrimination that other citizens enjoy - such as reduced school fees, public healthcare and priority access to public sector jobs. However, as residents of Saudi Arabia, they had access to schooling, healthcare and jobs in general.8

The RPD correctly concluded that the stateless Appellants did not present any allegations of risk or harm against Saudi Arabia on the basis of gender and the Appellants have not identified any errors committed by the RPD in this regard.

Having considered the evidence before me, I find that the Appellants have not established a serious possibility of harm, a risk to their lives, a risk of cruel or unusual punishment or a risk of torture as stateless Palestinians in the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia. Claim against Jordan

The RPD correctly found that there was not a serious possibility of persecution on a forward-looking basis, should the co-Appellant return to Jordan, and that she would not personally face a risk to life or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment or be subjected to a danger of torture upon return to Jordan.

The co-Appellant, wife of the Principal Appellant, holds Jordanian citizenship. She alleges that she was threatened by a member of a powerful tribal family in Jordan who sexually harassed her daughter because she reported the harassment to the police and insisted that charges be laid against him. She alleges that the police consistently tried to get her not to press charges because her daughter's harasser is powerful. She claims that she received threatening phone calls from the harasser who is to have threatened consequences for her actions.

The Appellants argue that the RPD failed to consider the cumulative effects of harassment in its decision. However, it did not reference where in its decision that the RPD failed to do so and in reference which issue. They have provided no specifics as to what effects of harassment the co-Appellant or any of the Appellants have suffered with respect to their claims, they have simply cited case law.9 Since I can identify no clear argument or error to address, I have not considered this issue in my decision.

Otherwise, the Appellants present two arguments alleging errors by the RPD - that it misconstrued key evidence in its findings, and that it failed to consider the effect of tribal law on the state protection apparatus in Jordan.

With respect to the RPD misconstruing key evidence in its findings related to Jordan, the RPD noted inconsistencies related to the date of the assault and the name of the assailant in the lawyer's letter. The Appellants clarified that there were errors in the lawyer's letter at the outset of the hearing and believe that the RPD erred by assigning little weight to the letter regardless. The lawyer's letter in question10 states that the co-Appellant requested that they follow up with the police on her behalf to request an incident report following the harassment incident that occurred on XXXX XXXX, 2016. At the outset of the hearing, the Appellants clarified that the letter mistakenly identified the date of the incident as XXXX XXXX XXXX instead of XXXX XXXX, 2016. When testifying, the co-Appellant spoke to an initial harassment incident that occurred on XXXX XXXX, 2016 as well as to follow up interactions with the police the next day. In light of that testimony, I do not find that the error in dates in the lawyer's letter is significant enough to do away with it as evidence. Though the RPD spoke to inconsistencies in the name of the assailant in the letter, it did not clarify what was the inconsistency. In the letter, the lawyer speaks to a Mr. XXXX XXXX XXXX. In their Basis of Claim (BOC) forms, the Appellants speak to being harassed by the XXXX family. During testimony, the Appellants explained that there are many English spellings for the same name when translated from Arabic. I do not find that the difference in spelling in this case is significant enough to do away with the lawyer's letter as evidence.

However, I do not find that the lawyer's letter is evidence that the XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX family is a powerful family in Jordan or that the letter is evidence that the Appellants are being harassed by that family. In the letter, the lawyer speaks to being informed of the harassment by the co-Appellant. The lawyer's actions are limited to trying to obtain a police incident report without success. Therefore, the RPD did not err in assigning little weight to the letter with respect to the co-Appellant's allegations of being targeted by a wealthy family.11

The Appellants also argue that the RPD erred by concluding that Jordan has a functioning state protection mechanism and that there is insufficient credible evidence of similarly situated individuals who did not receive state protection. The Appellants contend that evidence which they submitted shows that powerful tribal families have great influence over the state apparatus. I find that the RPD correctly concluded that the Appellants had not established that the XXXX family was able to control the state apparatus in order to harm the Appellants. Moreover, I find that upon reviewing the documentary evidence, the RPD correctly determined that the Appellants have not rebutted the presumption of state protection.12 The Appellants have submitted a series of articles speaking to the situation of tribal law in Jordan generally.13 Some of those articles establish that Jordanians sometimes opt to have their disputes resolved in tribal courts, even if Jordanian law does not officially recognize tribal courts in its justice system, and that this is a threat to Jordan's sovereignty as a state. One article confirms that Jordan has "a respected judiciary, a strong police force and intelligence service, and a powerful, well-equipped army... and is making progress towards empowering women and bridging the gender divide in society."14 The articles in question support, rather than rebut, the RPD's analysis which I deem to be correct. They confirm that while Jordan should be wary of tribal powers in the justice system, that it maintains control over the state protection apparatus. Moreover, the articles do not serve to confirm that the XXXX family can or has unduly influenced the state apparatus against the co-Appellant or her family.
The Appellants have identified no other errors with respect to the RPD's analysis as it relates to the co-Appellant's claim against Jordan and I have not identified any additional errors.

The RAD dismisses the appeal and confirms the decision of the RPD that the Appellants are neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection, pursuant to section 111(1)(a) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).
